lessons.culture: In the Gulf a morning starts with "صباح الخير" answered by "صباح النور", and a small cup of gahwa (light Arabic coffee, often with dates) before leaving the house is close to universal, even on a rushed morning.

exercises.prompt: Someone says to you: "صباح الخير". Reply naturally.

too_formal.item: صباح الخير عليكم ورحمة الله وبركاته
too_formal.feedback: Correct but far more elaborate than the everyday morning reply.

exercises.tip: The fixed everyday reply to "صباح الخير" is "صباح النور".

exercises.prompt: Someone asks you: "كم الساعة الحين؟" Answer that it's seven o'clock.

too_formal.feedback: A bookish way to say the time; nobody says it like this out loud.

exercises.tip: "الساعة + number" is the everyday pattern for telling the time.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence: "أبي _____ قبل كل شي." English meaning: I want coffee first thing.

too_formal.feedback: More explicit and formal than the simple everyday word.

exercises.tip: "أبي" is the Gulf "I want"; coffee is said "gahwa" with the ق as a hard g.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence: "الصبح بدري الجو بارد _____." English meaning: Early morning it is very cold.

too_formal.feedback: "جدا" is correct but written; Gulf speech says "وايد" (Kuwait also "واجد").

exercises.tip: "وايد" means "a lot / very" and comes after the word it strengthens.

exercises.prompt: Translate into Gulf Arabic: "I woke up early."

too_formal.feedback: Correct meaning, but this is written Arabic, not what people say out loud in the Gulf.

exercises.tip: "صحيت" is the everyday Gulf verb for "I woke up".

exercises.prompt: Translate: "I missed the bus."

too_formal.feedback: Grammatical but far too formal for complaining about a bus.

exercises.tip: "فاتني" is used for missing a bus, a flight, or any chance that passed.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "I'm still sleepy."

too_formal.feedback: Textbook Arabic; "للحين" is the natural Gulf word for "still".

exercises.tip: "للحين" before an adjective is how "still ..." is said in the Gulf.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence means "I left for work"?

too_formal.feedback: Correct meaning, but this is written Arabic, not what people say out loud in the Gulf.

exercises.tip: "دوام" is the everyday Gulf word for work hours or the workplace.

exercises.tip: "صباح النور" and "صباح الورد" are both natural replies.

exercises.prompt: Put these words in a natural order: "بدري / للدوام / طلعت"

too_formal.feedback: Correct meaning, but this is written Arabic, not what people say out loud in the Gulf.

exercises.tip: Verb, then place, then time is the natural spoken order here.

lessons.culture: Gulf offices run on "دوام" (working hours), and colleagues often go out for lunch together or have tea and gahwa sent to the desk; a favour is met with "تسلم" or "الله يخليك".

exercises.prompt: Your colleague asks: "وين تتغدى اليوم؟" Say you eat at the restaurant next to the office.

accepted: أتغدى في المطعم اللي جنب الدوام

too_formal.item: أتناول الغداء في المطعم المجاور للمكتب
too_formal.feedback: Correct, but this is the written register, not office talk.

exercises.tip: "اللي" is the Gulf "which/that"; "جنب" means "next to".

exercises.prompt: A colleague says: "أقدر آخذ استراحة؟" Reply yes.

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but flat and stiff for a friendly workplace.

exercises.tip: "خذ راحتك" literally "take your comfort", meaning take as long as you need.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence: "عندي _____ الساعة عشرة." English meaning: I have a meeting at ten.

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but "لدي" and "العاشرة" are written style; speech says "عندي" and "عشرة".

exercises.tip: "عندي" is "I have", and the hour is a plain number: "الساعة عشرة".

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence: "لازم أخلص هالشغلة قبل _____." English meaning: I have to finish this task before noon.

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but not how anyone names noon in a sentence like this.

exercises.tip: "الظهر" is noon and also the time of the midday prayer.

exercises.prompt: Translate into Gulf Arabic: "I'm hungry, I want to eat something."

too_formal.item: أنا جائع وأريد أن آكل شيئا
too_formal.feedback: Correct meaning, but this is written Arabic, not what people say out loud in the Gulf.

exercises.tip: "أبي" is "I want" and "شي" is "something", both very Gulf.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "I'm looking for my pen."

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but "أبحث" is written style; "أدور" is what is said.

exercises.tip: "أدور" is the everyday Gulf verb for "look for".

too_formal.feedback: Correct meaning, but this is written Arabic, not what people say out loud in the Gulf.

exercises.tip: "خلصت" is "I finished" in everyday speech.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence means "I have a lot of work now"?

too_formal.feedback: Correct meaning, but this is written Arabic, not what people say out loud in the Gulf.

exercises.tip: "وايد" means "a lot" and "الحين" means "now".

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but "سأتصل بك" is written; speech uses "بـ" for the future.

exercises.tip: "بـ" before the verb marks the future: "بتصل" is "I will call".

exercises.tip: "شوي" softens the feeling: "a little tired".

lessons.culture: Gulf evenings are the social time: the heat eases, families walk or drive out, and many people visit relatives or a majlis after the sunset prayer. Good night is "تصبح على خير" answered "وإنت من أهله", and plans are usually followed by "إن شاء الله".

exercises.prompt: Someone says to you: "مساء الخير". Reply naturally.

too_formal.feedback: Correct but longer and more ceremonial than the everyday reply.

exercises.tip: As in the morning, the reply changes the word: "مساء النور".

exercises.prompt: Someone says to you: "تصبح على خير". Reply naturally.

too_formal.feedback: Fine as a wish, but the fixed reply is "وإنت من أهله".

exercises.tip: Literally "and you are of its people"; use "وإنتي" to a woman.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence: "أبي _____ لأني تعبان." English meaning: I want to shower because I'm tired.

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but "أغتسل" is a formal or religious washing word.

exercises.tip: "أتروش" comes from the word "shower" and is very common in the Gulf.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence: "الجو حلو _____." English meaning: The weather is nice in the evening.

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but the full "المساء" is the written form; speech drops the final hamza and says "المسا".

exercises.tip: "المسا" is the evening; "بالليل" (at night) is also heard for a cool late evening.

exercises.prompt: Translate into Gulf Arabic: "I came back home."

too_formal.feedback: Correct meaning, but this is written Arabic, not what people say out loud in the Gulf.

exercises.tip: "البيت" is the everyday word for home; "المنزل" is written.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "What will we eat for dinner?"

too_formal.feedback: Correct meaning, but this is written Arabic, not what people say out loud in the Gulf.

exercises.tip: "شو" is "what" (Kuwait also "شنو"), and "بن" makes it "we will".

exercises.prompt: Translate: "I'll sleep early tonight."

too_formal.feedback: Correct meaning, but this is written Arabic, not what people say out loud in the Gulf.

exercises.tip: "بنام" is "I will sleep": the future "ب" joins straight onto the verb.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence means "Let's go out for a little walk"?

too_formal.feedback: Correct meaning, but this is written Arabic, not what people say out loud in the Gulf.

exercises.tip: "خلنا" starts a suggestion: "let us".

exercises.prompt: Which sentence means "I saw my friends in the evening"?

too_formal.feedback: Correct meaning, but this is written Arabic, not what people say out loud in the Gulf.

exercises.tip: "ربعي" means "my friends, my group" and is very Gulf.

exercises.prompt: Put these words in a natural order: "أهلي / أبي / أكلم"

too_formal.feedback: Correct meaning, but this is written Arabic, not what people say out loud in the Gulf.

exercises.tip: "أبي" plus a verb is "I want to ...".

lessons.culture: Friday is the day of Jumu'ah prayer and family time across the Gulf. Kuwait keeps Friday and Saturday as its weekend, while the UAE moved to a Saturday and Sunday weekend with a short Friday, so "الويكند" (the weekend) is the everyday word for both.

challenge.title: Plan Your Week in Gulf Arabic
challenge.instructions: Write and say a short conversation about a day and the week ahead, at least 10 lines. It must include a morning greeting and its reply, a question about the time, a statement about being tired or sleepy, an evening greeting and its reply, the good-night exchange, a question about a day of the week or a meeting time, and a plan for the weekend. Use at least 8 target phrases from Unit 7.
required_elements: A morning greeting using صباح الخير and its reply صباح النور.
A statement about waking up or being sleepy, using صحيت بدري or للحين نعسان.
A question using كم الساعة الحين؟ and a time answer.
A statement about being tired or having a lot of work, using تعبت or عندي شغل وايد.
An evening greeting using مساء الخير and its reply مساء النور.
The good-night exchange using تصبح على خير and وإنت من أهله.
A question using متى؟ and its answer.
A statement naming at least two days of the week.
A plan for the weekend using الويكند.
At least one invitation or suggestion, such as تبي تجي؟ or خلنا نطلع.

dialogue.english: Fine, what do you plan to do on the weekend?

dialogue.speaker: Khalid
dialogue.arabic: يوم الخميس أشوف ربعي، ويوم السبت نروح السوق.
dialogue.transliteration: yoom il-khamiis ashoof rab3i, w yoom is-sabt nroo7 is-soog.
dialogue.english: On Thursday I see my friends, and on Saturday we go to the market.

dialogue.speaker: Mariam
dialogue.english: Good night, see you tomorrow.

dialogue.speaker: Khalid
dialogue.english: And you too.
